annotations.description: Stadium Headliner is a 1/1 that creates attacking tokens with Mobilize 1, and can sacrifice itself to deal damage equal to creatures controlled. While it's only a 1/1, it can snowball value by creating tokens each attack, and its sacrifice ability could become relevant. Get Lost would cleanly remove it at the cost of giving opponent two Map tokens. However, the opponent only has one Mountain and the Headliner is a low-impact threat at this stage. The Map tokens could help the opponent find lands and improve card quality. With two copies of No More Lies in hand, the player may prefer to hold up countermagic for more impactful threats. Not using Get Lost here is defensible but worth considering since the Headliner's Mobilize triggers add up and the sacrifice ability scales with creature count.

annotations.betterLine: Could have cast Get Lost targeting Stadium Headliner to prevent incremental token value from Mobilize triggers, though holding mana for No More Lies on turn 3 is also reasonable.

annotations.description: Playing Fire Nation Palace before combat with an aggressive deck holding combat tricks (Full Bore, Turn Inside Out, Dreadmaw's Ire) and a Stadium Headliner ready to attack. While Fire Nation Palace enters untapped (since a basic Mountain is controlled), the player should consider whether attacking first with Stadium Headliner before playing the land would be better to avoid giving information. More importantly, the player could consider plotting Slickshot Show-Off this turn (costs 1R, which they have with Mountain + Fire Nation Palace), but that's actually fine since they need to play the land first to have the mana. The land play itself is reasonable, but there's a question of whether Mountain would have been better to keep open more flexible mana options and save Fire Nation Palace for later when its firebending ability becomes relevant. However, Fire Nation Palace entering untapped and providing red mana is functionally similar to Mountain here, and plotting Slickshot Show-Off is enabled either way.

Since Slickshot has haste naturally, plotting it doesn't gain the haste benefit (it already has it). The main advantage of plotting is casting it for free on a later turn to save mana for pump spells. However, with Stadium Headliner already on board ready to attack, the player could have held the Slickshot and played the Mountain from hand first (ensuring the land drop), then attacked with Stadium Headliner this turn. By plotting now, they tap out and can't use Fire Nation Palace's firebending ability or hold up any combat tricks. More importantly, they should play their Mountain land first before spending mana - though in this case plotting does use exactly 2 mana (1R) and they have Mountain + Fire Nation Palace available. The sequencing of plotting before playing the Mountain land drop is the real issue - they should play Mountain first to have more options, then decide whether to plot or just cast Slickshot next turn with pump spell mana available.

annotations.betterLine: Play Mountain from hand first (ensuring the land drop is not missed), then plot Slickshot Show-Off using two of the three available lands, keeping one land untapped for potential interaction or at minimum not risking forgetting the land drop.

annotations.description: Using Get Lost on Stadium Headliner (a 4/3 creature) on turn 3 when the opponent is tapped out gives them two Map tokens, which provide card selection advantage. With two copies of No More Lies in hand and only 2 lands (both Floodfarm Verge), the player could instead hold up No More Lies next turn to counter the opponent's next threat while developing their mana. Stadium Headliner is a reasonable threat to remove, but spending premium removal this early when holding counterspells and the opponent is tapped out (meaning they can't pressure immediately next turn without casting something new) is debatable. The Map tokens given are real value for an aggressive red deck.

annotations.description: Casting Emberheart Challenger before combat is suboptimal when holding three combat tricks (Dreadmaw's Ire, Full Bore, Turn Inside Out). Slickshot Show-Off is already on the battlefield with flying and haste. By casting a creature before combat, the player misses the opportunity to pump Slickshot with noncreature spells during combat for maximum damage. Additionally, casting Emberheart Challenger pre-combat telegraphs the threat and doesn't trigger Slickshot's pump ability (since it's a creature spell). The opponent has only 2 tapped lands, so there's no interaction to worry about. The better line is to attack with Slickshot first, then use combat tricks to pump it, and cast Emberheart Challenger post-combat (it has haste so it could attack, but playing tricks on Slickshot's attack is likely higher damage output).

annotations.betterLine: Move to combat, attack with Slickshot Show-Off, and use noncreature pump spells (Turn Inside Out, Full Bore, Dreadmaw's Ire) during combat to maximize Slickshot's damage via its +2/+0 trigger per noncreature spell. Cast Emberheart Challenger post-combat if desired. With Slickshot at 1/2 flying, casting even two pump spells during combat would give it +4/+0 from triggers plus the pump effects themselves for massive damage.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Full Bore targeting Emberheart Challenger for 9 total damage plus Valiant trigger (exile top card for potential extra play), preserving Dreadmaw's Ire for a future turn where trample matters.

annotations.description: Slickshot Show-Off is arguably the more dangerous threat here. Emberheart Challenger is a 2/2 with haste and prowess (+1/+1 per noncreature spell), which is less explosive. The opponent already used Dreadmaw's Ire from the graveyard, suggesting they're building around combat tricks with Slickshot. At 10 life, Grok4F Valley is particularly vulnerable to Slickshot's flying burst damage since they have no creatures to block flyers.
